utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Welcome back, Ambassador. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, may I just ask the usher, Mr. Usher, to bring me the lectern if possible, since we only have one to go around in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Alajbeg.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try to ask you some questions that I did not have time to ask the last time you testified before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we please briefly go back to your statement, the statement you gave to the investigators of the International Criminal Tribunal, specifically to the portion of your statement referring to the situation concerning the presidency of the former Yugoslavia. In your statement you say that: "As of the 8th of October, it was difficult to imagine that the SFRY would continue to exist in any way, given the fact that among other things the presidency itself had ceased to function." Tell me, Madam, why did Stipe Mesic remain a member of the presidency until as late as the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the presidency, but also the other federal organs had ceased to function at that time. This also applies to the JNA, to the presidency, to the constitutional court of the SFRY, as well as the parliament. I think the Badinter Commission focused on that in its opinion number 1, ascertaining the fact that Yugoslavia was disintegrating, also due to the malfunctioning of the federal bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, my question was a different one. Let us not waste time today. My question was why did Stipe Mesic remain in the presidency until as late as the 5th of December. If you could please focus on my questions and provide accurate answers in as far as you can, Madam.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that Croatia had become a sovereign independent state and regardless of the fact that all action taken by the federal bodies had been taken pursuant to decisions of the parliament and were later declared null and void by the parliament, not only Stipe Mesic but rather also other high officials remained in contact with the federal bodies and Mesic remained as a member of the presidency, precisely because the aggression against Croatia had not ceased. It seemed at the time and certain agreements were made that the aggression would stop and that the JNA would withdraw. It was precisely because of that in late 1991 that the situation was very difficult for Croatia. And that's when the number of victims reached its peak. That was nothing unusual at the time and even President Tudjman himself said on a number of occasions, I would be prepared to deal with the devil himself just for the situation to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, Stipe Mesic, did he remain a member of the presidency of the SFRY until as late as the 5th of December and did he discharge his duties as the president of the presidency of the SFRY? Please answer concisely if you can, yes or no, if you know.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes, he remained in that position but he did not discharge his duties because that was made impossible for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me in the meantime in his position, in his capacity as president of the SFRY he attended international meetings.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the reasons that I've already given. It is indeed possible that he did take part in international meetings. But all the meetings he attended after that date, the sole reason was his attempt to prevent aggression and to make it possible for the army to withdraw from Croatia. Another thing I wish to point out is that on the 8th or on the 7th, more specifically, of October, Stipe Mesic spoke in the parliamentary assembly at Strasbourg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question, Madam.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best. He spoke on behalf of the sovereign state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether he signed any documents between the 8th of October and the 5th of December in his capacity as the president of the SFRY presidency?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, simply because I don't know what he signed throughout that period of time. However, there were documents that had to do with cessation of hostilities against Croatia. He probably signed a number of those, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he sign any documents in his capacity as the president of the presidency of the SFRY or on behalf of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know which specific documents he signed. That was not within my purview of activity. This is possible. It is possible that he signed some documents, but not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see in the Official Gazette of the SFRY any documents that were signed by Stipe Mesic in his capacity as president of the presidency of the SFRY in the period that we are referring to, ending on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. Nothing occurs to me right now, no document that was published in the Official Gazette of the SFRY at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown exhibit P20, two binders of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, can you please look at tab 1 in binder 1, tab 1, binder 1. Can you please find the document that has been marked 589, conclusions on the political conditions obtaining -- in the Republic of Croatia. The date of the document is 17th of April, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was published on the 23rd of April, 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 6 of this document. In view of what paragraph 6 states, is it not obvious that as early as April 1991 Croatia was seeking the destruction of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that Croatia at that time was prepared to insist on its total sovereignty as a state, its independence; however, the word "destruction of the SFRY" is I think an inappropriate description. It was not Croatia's intention to destroy the SFRY, but rather to fight for its independence, which was clearly expressed in the Croatian constitution that had been adopted in December 1990, which clearly stated that Croatia was a sovereign and independent state, which through agreements with the other republics and other sovereign subjects could form associations and alliances. This was the question posed at the April referendum also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please provide brief answers so we can finish today. Can you please look at item 7. Can you tell me what was it at that time that was unconstitutional about the presidency of the SFRY? What unconstitutionality are we talking about back in April 1991, as far as the composition of the presidency of the SFRY is concerned, as described by item 7?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically remember what this refers to, but I think it probably refers to the autonomous regions, the autonomous provinces, and I think that's what the problem was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the presidency made up of the presidents of all the individual republics at the time, presidents of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and Macedonia took work in the presidency at the time, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It comprised representatives of all the individual republics; however, I know that back then talks were being held regarding the composition of the presidency because the presidency had been put together in such a way that there are three members from the then-republic of Serbia, because both the autonomous provinces and the republic of Serbia were entitled to one representative each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Serbia, you say, had three members. Did this run counter to the constitution of Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it probably ran counter to what was being widely debated at the time, so this wording about unconstitutional composition -- I'm not sure if this refers to a legal aspect or to a factual aspect of the situation where a particular appointee was appointed in a way that was not constitutional. I cannot answer this specific question right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have a situation where three members of the SFRY presidency and that is perfectly constitutional. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that it was in compliance with the then-constitution, because the autonomous provinces were entitled to their own representatives, but there may have been another situation where someone was appointed in a way which was not constitutional, but I can't remember right now. That's why I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you referred to a number of different institutions that were part of the framework of the SFRY which ceased to exist or function in that year. In continuation of item 7, the item that we're looking at, is it not stated very clearly that the parliament of the Republic of Croatia wants the Yugoslav constitutional court to take certain measures. Does this mean that the constitutional court should adopt decisions and that these decisions will then be regarded by the Republic of Croatia as legal and legitimate?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This still falls short of meaning, that the Republic of Croatia is not a sovereign state, and it doesn't mean that Croatia does not recognise these institutions at the time. Back then, the possibility of having a confederation was still widely debated and the possibility to deal with the crisis by negotiating on the ground and politically. As I said in my testimony, Croatia and Slovenia were working on a concept of a confederal agreement. This is a fact. This was after all a well-known and published fact. It had eight chapters, this agreement. Croatia was in negotiations with Slovenia but I would say Croatia was more serious about it. They were reviewing a situation where a confederal concept and a smooth transition to a confederal concept would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, if we keep on talking like this it will take days for us to finish this cross-examination. Please if you can focus on my question which had to do with the constitutional court. Can we partially or fully deny the fact that the constitutional court was legal and legitimate at the time. Did Croatia at that time recognise the legal and legitimate nature of the constitutional court of Yugoslavia or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it still did, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this document marked -- it is from the same Official Gazette. It is marked 598. This is a law amending the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately there is no English translation of this document in the copy which you have, although it does exist in the B/C/S version and we will be providing a copy for you. But I'd like to use -- avail myself of the presence of this witness to deal with this question. But we will be providing the document in English to you shortly. I do not know why this hasn't been done, because the text obviously exists here in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. And could I just remind you while we're interrupting you questions of the importance of pausing until the translation finishes before you move on to the next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, do you see this document, 598, and can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is? Can you read out the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Law amending the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to read out for the Trial Chamber article 25A of this law.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "To discharge duties from article 1 from item 2 of this law, the national guards corps is hereby established. The president of the republic shall determine the number of members and the organisation of the national guard on the proposal of the ministry of defence and the ministry of the interior. Regulations on the training of members of the national guard corps shall be brought by the minister of defence. The national guard corps shall be active throughout the territory of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read the first paragraph of article 25B.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The national guard corps is a professional, uniformed armed formation of a military organisation for defence and police duties."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please also read out article 25C.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Units of the national guards corps shall be commanded by the Ministry of Defence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also be so kind as to concur with me in my view that this law was adopted on the 18th of April, 1991, which you can see at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me from the standpoint of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia then in force, was the founding of such an armed formation as this one unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't, because the constitution of the Republic of Croatia was in force at the time, which was -- which declared itself as being above, senior to the SFRY constitution, so that the founding of this army -- armed foundation was in keeping with the constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the constitution -- did the constitution of the Republic of Serbia envisage the existence of such an armed formation. The constitution of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have it before me now. I suppose that it did because this was a sovereign state which envisaged -- made provision for all its -- prerogatives of sovereignty, including its right to defence and also its own armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that the forming of such an armed formation was in contravention of the SFRY constitution at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree insomuch as it was not material. It was in keeping with the Republic of Croatia, which was -- which took precedence over the SFRY constitution in the sense that the people in the dense sovereign state exercised their sovereign rights through their republic. So that the constitution of the republic could not be secondary in nature in respect to the SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you negating, Madam, the hierarchy of the legal acts in the country which at that time was called the SFRY, where the constitution was the supreme legal act and then only followed all others?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the republican constitution was the supreme legal act in the territory of the republic, and this law pertained to the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the federal constitution made provision for armed forces as the JNA and the Territorial Defence as the sole armed formations in the territory of the SFRY, do you still assert that in the territory of a member republic there could exist another armed formation and still be legal and legitimate?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If it was in accordance with the republican constitution and the republican constitution did exist at the time. This whole thing about the founding of armed and police forces at that time should be observed in the proper context, and Croatia had to expedite the adoption of such regulations because it was attacked by what was called the joint army and it certainly was no joint army, seeing that it had attacked one of its own republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me, Madam, who was it that was attacked by the joint JNA army in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It attacked indirectly -- rather, it armed en masse parts of the population in Croatia. And already at that time, in April that is, there had broken out bloody conflicts in Plitvice and that is precisely what contributed to the speedy forming of police forces because we didn't have any weaponry for establishing any armed forces. And of course I'm saying this as a witness who only has indirect knowledge of this because I was not present at the time. I do know there was a large-scale clash at Plitvice at the time where many police forces -- Croatian police forces perished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not true, but this is not the subject of your testimony so we shall not dwell on this at this point. Tell me: How is it possible for an armed formation to be set up under the law on the interior, the law on internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time Croatia still did not have its own defence law, which it only adopted at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Distinguished Madam, please be so kind to take the second binder, P20, and take a look at it. The law on general people's defence, document number 1, tab 13. The law on general people's defence brought on the 2nd of February, 1991, and then after that the law on defence brought on the 20th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this is in tab 13 of exhibit P20, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these laws on defence, Madam?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The law on general people's defence is not a law on defence. These were republican regulations which only related to the so-called territorial units and territorial defence which was an institute of the former state which was beyond the law on defence proper. These were republican regulations so they were restricted in scope in terms of dealing only with territorial defence units which were not regular defence forces. So these are not the same regulations. It was only in September that the defence law was promulgated in Croatia. Now this is something else, this is the time when Croatia assumed upon itself to defend itself and formed its own armed forces, whereas the territorial defence is something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling me that the law on total people's defence that you spoke about in detail answering the questions of my colleague when she put them to you during the examination-in-chief is not the law which regulates questions of defence, is not a law --- and is not a law which precedes the law on Defence from September 1991. Would you please be so kind as to take a look in this law on the 20th of September, 1991, the transitional and the concluding provisions. Article 201 of the concluding and transitional provisions. Where it says: "After the coming into force of this law, the coming of this force -- the coming of this law into force shall supersede the previous law on defence, meaning that one law ceases to exist and introduces the other law which regulates the same field."

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You obviously do not understand the distinction between the general or total people's defence which is the territorial defence and the law on defence. These are two totally different concepts and two different notions. In the former state of Yugoslavia, there existed also a law on defence which had to do with the armed forces, with the JNA. It never had dealt with the general total people's defence, which was within the republican local competence and the republic's regulated. It involved the rights of the entities, enterprises, civil and legal persons, in case of any imminent danger, but this had to do with Territorial Defence, namely the protection of people and civilian persons. This was not a law treating the armed forces and the military. And if this law on defence which was inaugurated for the first time then in Croatia and was published in September 1991 superseded the previous law and rendered it invalid, that is only logical because there was no need for the former piece of legislation to exist anymore because this law regulated all pertinent issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, Mrs. Alajbeg, you say according to the 1991 constitution, Croatia is a sovereign state, the -- the 1990 constitution, why then this same parliament of Croatia which had adopted all the other documents that we are discussing about, why did it bring this law on national defence on the 2nd of February, 1991, which is to say two months prior to this document that we are now discussing from tabulator 2. And the constitutional ground is the same with the constitution from 1990. And you say that there is no continuity between these two legal acts?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that there is no continuity. What I'm saying is that it was rendered invalid. Put out of force doesn't mean anything. Namely, the law on total people's defence in this early period -- the fact that it was published in 1990, that early, means that only at the time Croatia did not -- it did not occur to Croatia that it could be attacked in any way by the JNA at that -- that is what it shows. We were thinking about a confederal union at the time, about a peaceful negotiated agreement between the sovereign republics. In view of the fact that at a later stage what did happen was an attack on Croatia, which involved many casualties and dead and wounded people. It went without saying that this concept of Territorial Defence was no longer pertinent and that we had to think about forming our own defensive forces. Because not only would not the Territorial Defence function and could not function in such a state of affairs, but in this time, mid-1990, all the weapons of the Territorial Defence had been seized from it under orders of the then-federal minister of defence. Accordingly, that law could not be implemented because not -- even the minimum of arms which the Territorial Defence normally had had, had been seized. So it was pointless at that time to have a Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am compelled to ask for your assistance. I would like to stick to legal regulations and provisions here, the two binders that Madam Witness is talking about. If we start hearing testimony on what went on precisely at the time from Ms. Alajbeg and her views on it, I'll take days to finish my cross-examination. I only wish to discuss documents here, but if the witness goes on providing such extensive answers, I must say that I'll not be able to complete all my documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my part, by your leave, Your Honours, I ask to be allowed to place things into perspective. At this time there was a disintegration of the legal and political system. The text must be interpreted in its proper context, otherwise various misreadings might be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a fundamental tension here between your intention as a questioner, Mr. Petrovic, and the view held by the witness. It is at the core of this case, in some respects, and it will be for this Chamber to determine it. I think it would be improper of the Chamber to try and restrict the witness to answering in your context solely. And she may want to answer your question by including her view of the circumstances. At the same time, though, Ms. Alajbeg, you are doing that and more. You are giving extremely extensive answers. I think you can convey your message much more succinctly than is happening to date. Mr. Petrovic is being placed under time constraints to ensure that you can conclude your evidence today. And it would be to your advantage and his and the Chamber's if you were able to put your viewpoint in answer succinctly and we would be grateful if you would do that. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, can we now please move on to tab 2 of Exhibit P20. Let us look at document 646.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under which number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 646, the decision to have a referendum dated 25th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said binder 2, so that's why --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's tab 2 in binder 1. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you please tell me the following: This question posed by the referendum, a question that we see here, why was the word "independent" completely omitted from the question? The word "independent." The only terms given here are "sovereign" and "autonomous."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before the witness answers this question, Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the translation of the same document, which you have before you I believe. It says: "Sovereign and independent state." In the Croatian text or in the B/C/S language, if you like, "independent" is "independent." And the word "samostalan" is a different word from the word "independent"; it has a different meaning. It would mean roughly self-managing or self-organising; certainly not independent. The equivalent would be perhaps home rule. So the words samostalan and nizavistan [phoen] are not synonymous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you tell me, please, with the question posed by the referendum at this point in time, why was the word "autonomous" and "sovereign" completely omitted and the word "independent" only crops up in September 1991 in the parlance of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a misinterpretation of the words "samostalan". It means what the word "independent" means in English and it certainly refers to no kind of home rule or anything that counsel is suggesting. It is my submission that "samostalan" means "independent" in English, therefore these are synonymous. Linguistically speaking there may be a slight distinction in terms of nuance, but the English phrase "independent state" means samostalan drzolaj [phoen], exactly as described by the question on referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question. Why is the word samostalan being used here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought that question had just been answered, Mr. Petrovic. The witness disagrees with your construction and takes the view that it is a correct use of language. I don't think that you and the witness could debate that for any longer, to any good purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a clear question ever asked of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia, whether they wished to live in an independent state of Republic of Croatia? This question, as posed here, is not a clear question, which is obvious if you look at the wording of the question.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This referendum question actually contains two subquestions, one of which refers exactly to this. As a sovereign and independent state, Croatia can enter associations with the other republics. And the latter part, whether the citizens wanted Croatia to stay within the framework of the SFRY as a single and unified federal state. These are not mutually exclusive, needless to say. The essential question is whether one wants independence, and the citizens' answer was yes. Furthermore, the citizens did not rule out the possibility that there might be an agreement with other sovereign subjects and enter possible associations. Croatia did not rule out this possibility at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that the citizens of the Republic of Croatia were never asked this specific question: Do you wish to live in the independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't agree with you on that one, because that's simply not true. The citizens of Croatia were given a choice if they wanted an independent state and they said: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, here it states the following: The Republic of Croatia as a sovereign and independent state guaranteeing full rights to Serbs and ethnic minority may enter associations with other -- with the other republics. Linguistically speaking this question is perfectly clear; there is no two parts to this question. Do you think that the Republic of Croatia as an independent and sovereign state can enter alliances with other sovereign states? I don't see a question there saying: Do you want an independent state of Croatia? So how come you see those two in the same question?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the referendum question consists of both parts. I think you keep failing to read the second part. And the latter part of the question is about the citizens of Croatia, that the citizens of Croatia want a sovereign and independent state. And this state may then choose to enter associations with other states, to form associations with other states, which is a conditio sine qua non without which the Croatian state cannot enter any other alliances or associations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me about the latter part of the question. What sort of a proposal is it by Serbia and Montenegro that had been proposed at the time? Who defined this proposal?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know at the time there was a proposal by Serbia and Montenegro for Yugoslavia to become as unitarian as possible and to have a referendum. As far as I know this was a proposal by Milosevic along the lines of the one man, one vote principle to apply throughout Yugoslavia. So the proposal was for Yugoslavia to become a more unitarian state than it had been up to that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This proposal was formulated and published somewhere? Anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that it was specifically voiced or formulated, but there were a number of official meetings where this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one man, one vote principle, is that an anti-democratical principle in legal terms?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not under the laws that were in force in Yugoslavia at the time. This is no democratic way to resolve these issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we please move on to tab 3, the same document -- same exhibit, rather. Can you look at this decision, 708 decision, and tell me if you can, please. 708, the 7th of May, 1991. Tell me, please, there are two items, two provisions, in this decision?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the one referring to the referendum, and there are two items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me in relation to the latter item, this item, does it correspond with the second question posed by the referendum?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to provide an accurate answer, I would like to go back to the referendum question. I believe this decision was adopted on the basis of the answer provided by the citizens at the referendum; therefore, the decision merely publishes the results of the referendum. In my opinion, it does not have to correspond, but it must reflect the citizens' will as expressed at the referendum, but does not necessarily reflect the questions as asked originally, the original referendum questions. That's my opinion at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me: As of the 27th of May, 1991, what did Croatia do in order to achieve -- what was the obligation of the presidency of the Republic of Croatia, based on the results of the referendum? What were the steps that were taken in good will to establish an association of sovereign states, starting with the 27th of May and then over the following months? What steps were taken that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we should turn this question around. What did Yugoslavia, that is Serbia and Montenegro, at the time do to stop that happening? We know that in May there was already the massacre at Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May and there were military operations under way in Croatia. On a massive scale already people were being armed, so there was no possibility to do that. But I do know that Croatia was doing its best at the time to have some sort of negotiations. Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia were not in favour of the confederal concept, that Slovenia and Croatia had tabled at the time. They were favouring the so-called asymmetrical confederation. There was no consensus on that, and as far as I know Milosevic categorically refused any possibility of consensus as regarded the issue of the confederation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fortunately we here are not at all interested in Milosevic. So please tell me, what did the Republic of Croatia undertake to the effect of what the decision of the referendum stated? If you do not know, then please tell me so so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in consultations between the president of the republic at the time, the consultations of the presidents of the republics at the time, that there was a lot of talk about it. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now please move on to tab 4, the same exhibit, and take a look at document number 872. This is the constitutional decision on the sovereignty and the independence of the Republic of Croatia. And look at article 2 of this decision, paragraph 2 of this article which reads: "The Croatian republic is instituting procedure for its international recognition." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did at the time Croatia indeed initiate this procedure, as stated in this decision?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know we have to bear in mind the fact that the jurists who drew up the decision at the time were not all that precise. For instance, I myself who deal in international law would have never formulated it thus, because this is not a procedure that can be initiated by a state. This is a totally different process. A state itself cannot engineer recognition as it were. This is something which is initiated by others so that from the international law standpoint this is not the most fortunate of formulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the effects, if you know, of this formulation, please?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the recognition procedure evolved outside this framework. The Republic of Croatia could, so to speak, lobby for it. But its recognition on the part of individual states only ensued when those states were fully satisfied and convinced that they should indeed do so. There is no procedure of recognition, no legal procedure of recognition, as such. It doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though it does not exist, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia was asking for one.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was more by way of an instruction to the executive branch, to the officials in Croatia, as to what they should do in terms of working to promote the truth, I should say, about Croatia at the time, and to promote the need to draw attention to Croatia and its problems. In other words, the wish of the Croatian people expressed at the referendum for their autonomy and independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said an instruction based on the referendum. Does this instruction refer to the president of the presidency of this SFRY from the Republic of Croatia who -- Stipe Mesic, the prime minister at the time, who was also from the Republic of Croatia, Markovic the minister of defence who was from the Republic of Croatia at the time, Veljko Kadijevic; the minister of foreign affairs who was also from the Republic of Croatia at the time, Mr. Budimir Loncar -- or did this instruction already refer to -- did it refer to all of them or did it not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parliament of Croatia addressed this call to all whom -- and those who thought that the call did refer to them in fact followed -- acted accordingly. And those who didn't did not. While I did say instructions, but it was rather a call addressed to all these factors to work along these lines, all those who should engage -- be engaged along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So may I conclude that none of these factors that I mentioned, including you, did not consider that there was any scope for any work along those lines on that basis in fact?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in a way we had already started working on that, because when the armed conflicts broke out and the first victims fell, one could not remain passive. We were all involved in some sort of a procedure, because we sought to spread the truth about what was going on. And this is the effort that we who were working outside Croatia also shared in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that as of the 25th of June, as federal regulations ceased to be applied in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say yes, had it not been for the moratorium or the suspension of that decision. Namely, I've already put forward here my thesis that in fact I considered sovereignty and independence for Slovenia and Croatia to have already started on the 25th of June. But we also know that the Brioni declaration suspended that decision for a period of three months and that later the date of the succession or in translation of independence in the broader sense was only reckoned after the three months had elapsed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the context of what you've just said please take a look at the article 4 of the same constitutional decision which reads: "In the area of the Republic of Croatia are valid laws which have been brought by the parliament of Croatia and until the end and the disassociation of republics, also federal regulations which have not been put out of force."

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, put out of force for the Republic of Croatia. Because not only at that time but also later while passing its own legislation, the Republic of Croatia often accepted and applied federal regulations. But as its own pieces of legislation. Meaning federal regulations that had been accepted by the Republic of Croatia. So this are -- these are the pieces of legislation which are meant there, not meaning that the federal legislation was applicable at the same time in Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Distinguished Madam, we are jurists. We are here interpreting juristic acts and I'm asking you for an interpretation of this document which does not provide this clarification which you have given us but rather says: "Federal regulations shall also be applied." That is what it says. There is no question, at least in this legal document, of the adoption of these regulations as internal documents or of any other legal procedure. What it says is: "The direct application of federal regulations."

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This simply is perhaps not adequately phrased here, because this document is very brief. But later practice shows that all regulations, precisely those which were applied in the Republic of Croatia, on the basis of this decision, that article were applied by adopting a special law on the application of the federal law in question in full or in part. So practice demonstrated precisely what that meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in your opinion, practice is one thing and the constitutional law, the supreme constitutional act of a state after the constitution is something else. Or, in other words, practice ran counter to what was the constitutional law at the time, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The constitutional decision may have left something to be desired in terms of precision. But the interpretation of the decision by the parliament, which in fact adopted this decision, showed how the federal laws were to be applied in the territory in -- of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree, the constitutional law is imprecise, but it was implemented and built upon and characterised through practice, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a constitutional decision not a constitutional law, but we cannot say that the entire decision is imprecise. It is just a small portion which is not -- which leaves something to be desired in terms of precision. But it is also quite obvious that it refers to federal regulations which have not been rendered invalid which have not ceased to be inoperative. Meaning the Republic of Croatia is a catalyst for federal laws. It doesn't mean that federal laws are to be applied directly because they are federal laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Look at Article 5 of the same decision. Tell me in your opinion, Madam, does Article 5 constitute a one-sided decision making on the part of one personality, one fact of whether it is an internationally recognised state or not on its own state boundaries. That is my first question. And my second question is: Can the question of state borders be regulated unilaterally by an internal act of one entity?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- at the moment we are speaking about is an independent state, which became on autonomous independent state on the basis of a referendum and the will of its citizens. So I interpret this article exclusively as the wish of the Republic of Croatia to remain within its existing borders at the time without any claims or pretensions to any other territories or borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain to me the following: Can state borders be drawn unilaterally? What is the process of the drawing of state borders? Is that a one-sided decision by an entity, by state, by province, whatever you like? Or are state borders fixed in a different way?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not new borders. This is not a change of the Helsinki criteria. This is, in fact, a confirmation of the Helsinki criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please explain for us. What are the Helsinki criteria?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of the OSCE we know that there exists the Helsinki criteria which have to do with the not changing of borders by force. So these are established -- we just noted the existing borders of the Republic of Croatia, which on the basis of the will of its people and the right exercise by its people was proclaimed to be an independent state, which remained in its former or existing borders which it had before as a state that had joined the former Yugoslavia of its own volition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell the Trial Chamber, to what do the Helsinki charter, the Helsinki criteria refer? Do they refer to administrative units within states, or do they refer to the principle of the unchangeability of borders between internationally recognised states?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does refer to states, but at the time Croatia was a state. And that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please move on to document 875 at the same tabulator number. Declaration of independence and sovereignty of the state of Croatia. So please, if you look at item 1 or paragraph 1, which says, starting with 13 centuries of legal and state tradition between the Adriatic the Drava and Mirna rivers. Please tell me, the Croatian parliament in this declaration does it imply also Bosnia-Herzegovina territory to be included, if we bear in mind the geographical location of these rivers being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Even nowadays Croatia has the Adriatic and the rivers Drava and Mirna. These rivers run through Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When someone says "soil," or rather "territory" between the Drava, which is the border between Croatia and Hungary and the Adriatic on the other hand with the state territory of another state lying in between in its entirety. Can you explain how this is possible.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this requires any sort of explanation. To the north of Croatia you have the Drava river and in the south of Croatia there is the Adriatic sea. I'm not sure if there is any other way to describe this since they decided to describe it this way. Personally I would have done it in a different way perhaps. But since they started described things in this way, describing territory, then I don't think this constitutes a problem. Because we know that to the north we have the Drava river, then we have the Mora river, and to the south we have the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is there in between?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best part of Croatian. Croatia has an irregular shape but that falls short of meaning anything specific here in this context. It does not mean that everything that there is in between is simply Croatian. That is not stated anywhere here, not unambiguously, and I don't see a problem here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 4 of the same decision -- or rather, section 4, paragraph 3. My question to you is the following: You said in January when we had the same sort of discussion that the conditions for sovereignty and independence had been met already in June 1991. But here I can see the following words: "The declaration of a constitutional decision initiates the process of disassociation." Initiates the process, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, this is not necessarily a matter of wording, especially if you look at declarations. The wording is not always accurate. The main thing was that Croatia declared its independence. The main thing was that Croatia had determined its fate in terms of sovereignty and autonomy. It had its own regulations and its own laws. So my interpretation of this is: There was an agreement. Croatia was ready to enter an agreement with the remaining republics in order to possibly resolve their even, perhaps, shared fate through a different kind of arrangement, a confederal arrangement, or something like that. But remaining at the same time sovereign and independent. That's the essence of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decision on independence initiates the process of dissociation. Do you perhaps believe that the legislators were not wording their position with sufficient accuracy?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said. Because in initiating the process of dissociation, I would say through dissolution of relations or severance of relations we became a state and independence had been proclaimed and the state had its own constitution. This does not necessarily imply that all other kinds of relations with other entities in the area had been dissolved. We still have the question of state succession, even nowadays and a number of other problems that have not yet been resolved. So this refers to the process of disassociation, in terms of legally dealing with what remained there to be dealt with at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, the supreme organ in the Republic of Croatia which is in charge of authentically interpreting the legal documents of the parliament -- of the Croatian parliament, is that body the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the body which adopted the law should authentically interpret the law, however this is not a matter of interpretation. The decision itself is crystal clear. This is merely a declaration which in a very extensive fashion explains the situation surrounding the declaration of independence. It talks about historical connotations. It talks about a vision of a new state. Therefore, the character of this act is not that of a constitutional decision. This is in itself clear, perfectly clear. This is a declaration of an independent state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't this the third time in the last 15 minutes that you keep talking about inaccuracy in the wording of acts adopted by the supreme legislative authority of Croatia, and you attempt to provide your own interpretation of what the legislator wanted to suggest, but which is in stark contrast to the linguistic wording which is now before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe that linguistically speaking, everything is crystal clear. And everything that counsel has adopted -- every time he has adopted to twist an interpretation his way, to suit his needs, I don't think that was correct and authentic. I'm talking about these two norms here, not three norms but rather two norms, but this makes the decisions no less important, or the act in question for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next paragraph in section 4, which reads: "The proclamation of the constitutional decision on independence is a prerequisite for the Republic of Croatia to be recognised as an international entity. The president of Croatia and the Croatian government will take all necessary steps to achieve this." Do we here see the legislator wording himself in an inaccurate way, just like we said in reference to document 872 a while ago? Does it not seem that this is a bit superfluous perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very clear provision. There is nothing to be challenged here. It is only natural that everyone shall take steps to initiate this process. It doesn't mean anything in itself. Nothing special at least is implied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if some conditions are in place and if what you say is true, that this was a fact and not a matter of something being officially declared, then why the whole thing? Why all this?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because each state wants to have as much recognition in terms of declaration, even though the Badinter Commission stated that the creation of a state was a questio facti but every state wants to have it in terms of declaration and recognition done expressed by international factors and international entities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that a full seven months after this decision, Croatia was granted its first formal recognition if we discount at the moment the recognition granted by entities that themselves were not recognised at the time, such as Slovenia and Latvia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is wrong because Latvia proclaimed its independence in March 1991 and it was recognised as a full-fledged UN member in September of the same year. So Latvia was not exactly an unrecognised state. Before it was admitted as a member of the United Nations, there had been international agreements that had been concluded on diplomatic relations which had been in place before that time with the United States, with Germany, and with some other states that are part of the -- this Western world of ours. Therefore, Latvia and all the remaining Baltic countries had been granted full recognition by the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, which month are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about June. Here specifically, the recognition late July, on the part of Latvia. Latvia at that time had developed international relations and it was a fully-recognised entity by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's leave this issue aside for the time being. We will talk about that later. Let us not tire the Chamber with this now. Tell me now please: In addition to Latvia, who else?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we talked about Croatia's recognition at such great length the last time we talked about it. I'm not sure we should go into this again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need to go into the issue of Croatia's recognition again. I think we've been through that. But what I want to know as I see that in the meantime you have prepared yourself for this testimony, you have refreshed your memory of events. Have you been able to ascertain in the meantime whether there was anyone else who granted the Republic of Croatia recognition in the same period of time under discussion here. If you don't know, please say so?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've talked about this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at document 876, "Charter on the rights of Serbs and other ethnic groups in the Republic of Croatia".

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's tab 4 also, the last document. Madam, can you please tell me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 876, my apologies. Tab 4, the last document and the last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please be asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just look at it and then I'll ask you my question.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document in English here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we worked based on that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was this document a sufficient basis for the Republic of Croatia in terms of dealing with minority rights, ethnic minority rights. We are talking about a document dated June 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not sufficient basis. Croatia knew that it had to adopt this legal act, but obviously it had to go through a number of different revisions, which was subsequently done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it about this document that is still missing?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document in front of you, 876, what are its shortcomings, its drawbacks? What causes you to say that it had to undergo a number of revisions and amendments?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is anything fundamentally wrong about this document. The requirements of the international community in Europe kept increasing, and Croatia had to follow those requirements because we wanted to make sure that all the minorities enjoyed the same rights in a sovereign state like ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any criteria established, criteria that a state should comply with in order to become a state in relation to the -- its treatment of ethnic minorities?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the international criteria, criteria in terms of international law are enshrined in this document. That's not the problem. The problem was -- is that there was an attempt to make sure down to the smallest detail that the rights of minorities in Croatia at the time were respected and that the rights were granted, especially as regards the Serbian minority which was the largest single minority in Croatia. And that's why the international community kept asking for more and more and more. So there followed a number of documents that superseded this one and that were a good deal more extensive than the original document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that no clear criteria were presented by the international community but rather that these criteria were changed as we went along and that Croatia meanwhile always treated its minorities in the same way?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Croatia always declared that it wanted to protect its minorities according to the highest possible European standards. But Croatia was required to work on even the smallest details so that there was nothing at a later stage to cause any possible conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as the Croatian Ambassador in Brussels even today are still being asked about the status of the Serb minority in Croatia, even 15 years later. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is not only about the Serb minority. They are asking questions about minorities in general. This is always the case in areas where you have minorities. And ours is one such area. In each of the former republics which are states, independent states today, there are ethnic minorities and this a problem that these new states are facing. There is always the possibility of unrest. And that is why an attempt is being made, not only in relation to Croatia but in relation to all other states in the area to have a regulatory system that would eliminate tension in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at tab 9 of the same exhibit, the arbitration opinion number 5. Madam, please tell me -- please tell me, based on what's written in the arbitration commission opinion number 5: At the time -- in the period of time preceding this opinion, had the Republic of Croatia already met the requirements governing the recognition of new states in Europe and the former Soviet Union in reference to such issues as national minorities? I'm talking about the time before the arbitration commission opinion number 5.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, these criteria were increased and it has been established here that the constitutional law -- and we're not talking about the charter because several other legal acts had been adopted in the meantime. The constitutional law on the rights of minorities at the level of constitution and not merely at charter level, as we have seen. It is stated here that not everything that was contained in the draft convention of the 4th of November was embodied or incorporated by Croatia. This relates especially to the special status of Croatia. This is not about human rights, this is not about minority rights. This is about requests that were made to Croatia, peculiar requests, for -- and in reference to municipalities where we had the majority Serbian population. So that's what this was about; this was about special requests that were made at the time in terms of governance, in terms of education, but this overwrote -- of the general standards, I would say. So Croatia was being asked to make its constitutional law even better, even more detailed, which when asked to do so by the European Union, and Croatia duly complied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the constitutional law was imperfect and it needed amendments?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can you name any provision or regulation that you think is perfect at all. But Croatia was making a huge effort at the time. At the level of constitutional law there was an extensive law on the protection of minority rights. I would dare even to suggest that it's more extensive than any other such law in Europe in any other European state

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the main criteria for the recognition of new states in eastern Europe was the treatment of ethnic minorities. When did the Republic of Croatia adopt a constitutional law governing the rights of minorities?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minority rights were regulated through a number of different legal acts and regulations, not necessarily only by this constitutional law dated the 4th of December, 1991. This was not the first document adopted by the Croatian state to protect the ethnic minorities. This is just a very extensive and complex document that was perfected over time. But we started out speaking about the charter, which in its own way granted protection to the ethnic minorities and granted them rights. There were other such documents at the time. I can't remember now how many specifically, but I know that a great deal of care and attention was devoted to this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: European countries and the United States in the period of time under discussion until December 1991 considered that the conditions were not met with regard to ethnic minorities, and that as a result of noncompliance with that particular request the Republic of Croatia in its desire to become an internationally recognised state adopted the constitutional law on the 4th of December, thereby removing the drawbacks and shortcomings that had been pointed out by all civilised countries of the world?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This 4th of December constitutional law did not remove any drawbacks. It is clearly stated here that even this constitutional law has failed to fully incorporate all the requirements. There were further amendments made to this law, too. These amendments were a continuous process and this was continually pursued by Croatia over the years, but the requirements were becoming bigger and bigger and more precision was required in terms of defining protection for the ethnic minorities. But this was perfectly understandable in view of the situation on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were the requirements were regretting bigger and bigger, more ambitious while the situation on the ground and the standards of the protection of minority rights in Croatia on the ground did not follow suit. Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation on the ground showed that the ethnic minorities were easy to manipulate and it was necessary to define in detail the protection of minority rights. And that's why I said that the Croatian law on minority rights is perhaps the most extensive or -- and the most detailed that exists in Europe today or perhaps it is among the most comprehensive and most detailed laws. This reflected the need to allay the tensions between the minorities -- between the majority population and the ethnic minorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that this is not a result of dissatisfaction felt among the international entities with regard to the Croatian minority law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is perhaps a possibility, but there was a desire to prevent any undesirable developments at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this a convenient time to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it is indeed. We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, please look at tab 5. Declaration of the European union -- on the European Community, rather, on Yugoslavia from the 26th of -- from the 6th of March, 1991. Paragraph 6 -- 2. Does this decision state that according to the opinion of the European community a single and democratic Yugoslavia had the best prospects of integrating into the new Europe?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is no secret that the international community wanted to preserve Yugoslavia and that it wanted to see the crisis reconciled in a peaceful way. That is a matter of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this attitude about a single Yugoslavia, was it also repeated in their declaration of Yugoslavia of the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now please take a look at the declaration of the 7th of July, 1992, appendix 1. Take a look at the second -- no, rather the first section of this appendix, which reads: "Supervision of control of border crossings shall be assumed by the police of Slovenia." Is it true that this never, in fact, occurred, that this item 1 of appendix 1 was never carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This about it being assumed -- this duty being assumed by the Slovenian police, is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is whether it is true that this particular point, item 1, appendix 1, of the joint declaration of the 7th of July, 1992, which refers to the assumption of supervision of border crossings by the Slovenian police which was to act in accordance with the federal regulations was never carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Slovenia did take over the border crossings. Now, whether it acted in accordance with federal regulations, I could not say that with precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at paragraph 2, which deals with customs. And reads that: "Customs will remain a federal revenue source." Was this particular item of the joint declaration appendix abided by?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this refers to Slovenia. So it is hard for me to say what indeed had happened. I suppose that Slovenia did act as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Croatia paying customs proceeds as a federal revenue source at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the financial sphere, in view of the fact that the federal organs were not functioning, I believe that there existed formidable problems. Because at the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991, Serbia had raided, as it were, the financial system of the entire country with 1.700.000.000 being appropriated by it without the consent of the other republics. It simply illegally took that sum and this is known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Croatia pay its customs proceeds into the federal coffers?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that with precision. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Croatia a part of the payment operations system of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia throughout this period we are reviewing?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the decision on independence, it had been. After that, I am not quite sure how these financial flows went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the currency used in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the dinar until the fall when the Croatian dinar was introduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What currency was used in Croatia for -- say in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure when the Croatian dinar was introduced, whether it was in November or December. But at that time more or less it was introduced -- it was introduced more or less at that time precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the beginning of November, the Yugoslav dinar was the currency in circulation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. It probably was, which of course could mean anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, for instance, could it mean? Could the fact that the currency in Croatia on the 1st of November was the Yugoslav dinar, what could it mean?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could mean that there was no joint payment system. I already said it had been significantly disturbed by this incursion of the republic's -- individual republics, notably Serbia, into the payment system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you -- what does the fact that the currency in the Republic of Croatia was not a Croatian currency, but a Yugoslav currency, what does it exactly mean? In the period in question, of course.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that the state or the Republic of Croatia was using this currency does not mean that it cannot be an independent state. We have had instances with currencies being still operative in states that had become separated or independent states from other states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the phone code for the Republic of Croatia, telephone code?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me too much. I cannot remember exactly whether it was the same or different or -- really, at that time I cannot recall these technical details. I do know, however, that already in 1992 on the international level we had already resolved all these matters pertaining to communication links, et cetera, and all these such systems. But of course this was an exercise which was ongoing and couldn't be solved overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the registration plates or licence plates on cars in the fall of 1991 in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was not a single car without a CRO or at least a CR licence plate, although it had not already -- it had not been determined internationally by that time. But -- in this way it demonstrated their allegiance to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm asking you about the regulations which were in force at the time. What was the licence plate like at the time? It was just like the ones that were being used in 1990 or 1989?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I replied to you -- I do not own an automobile. I personally never used a licence plate and I could see that people were using these plates that I referred to earlier. It hadn't been officially verified, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at tab 6 of the document which is in front of you. Please take a look at the document marked as "Initiative of the assembly of the republic of Montenegro". And now take a look at the preamble of that document which reads: "Proceeding from the conclusions of the from the assembly of the republic of Montenegro, the assembly of the republic of Montenegro in accordance with principles of Article 4, Article 5, paragraph 4 of the constitution of Montenegro is instituting a -- launching an initiative for the fixing of the sea border".

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this initiative launched in the way envisaged under the constitution of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Article 5 of the constitution of the SFRY, the article which we discussed last time, which is the one which regulates by negotiation and agreement the relationship between states, i.e. Republics when it comes to the question of their shared borders?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Agreement is the criterion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come that you concluded that this act, which is based on the constitutional procedure of the existing state, constitutes an act of recognition of the Republic of Croatia on the part of the Republic of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was an implicit recognition, because at the time Montenegro was neither an independent state -- it wasn't an independent state. And this implied the recognition is obvious in item 1 from the simple fact that Croatia had decided to become a sovereign independent state is a fact which is taken into consideration. And it is stated so in item 1. So the fact that a state existed -- the state of Croatia, and then the fact that Montenegro felt that there was some unresolved issues pertaining to the issue of border which needed to be settled is referred to. Of course this was something that was not resolved at that point and certainly no changes of the borders took place. But my idea was to emphasise that Montenegro was aware of the fact that Croatia had become an independent state, and that is why it wanted to resolve precisely with it some of the relations which it felt were not settled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying these things as a jurist or as a politician and a journalist?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking as a juridical -- jurist, because this is actually circumstantial bit of evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- what Montenegro did was it strictly within the confines of the SFRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever said that it was not within the confines of the SFRY constitution, that initiative of Montenegro that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the fact that someone is undertaking a certain initiative, a certain action on the basis of the constitution, how can you conclude on that basis that someone is recognising something which is contrary to that same constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
