utterances.text: We are not talking here at all about something -- recognising something which is contrary to the constitution. Here we have Montenegro instituting a procedure, launching an initiative, on the basis of its own constitutional powers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this you see an implicit recognition, which was in contravention with the very fundaments on which this initiative is being launched --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the recognition of an existing state of affairs which is obvious from item 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then look at tab 7 now, please. So now please take a look at item 3 of this document contained therein, which reads: "The Republic of Croatia does not recognise as valid a single legal act which is -- represents anyone on behalf of the former federation of the SFRY." Tell me, why were not all the representatives of the Republic of Croatia withdrawn at that point if this was the attitude which was adopted?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot respond to your question, because I did not take any decisions as to the withdrawal of appointed persons. But I believe that this was a good-faith effort on the part of the Croatian side in order -- aimed at overcoming the situation, which by that time had become a veritable war. In order to resolve this also by way of these persons who were holding these posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which percentage of Croatian territory was then under the control of the authorities in Zagreb in October 1991, specifically?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, by that time those areas, independent areas, within the Croatian state had already been proclaimed. It was a well-known fact that those areas comprised about one-third of the entire Croatian territory, and 30 per cent of the population were Serbs. So the areas proclaimed as declared independent were actually far greater than the percentage of the population would have required. I would say about a third of the Croatian territory was under occupation. That's what they called it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the JNA at the time? Was it also stationed in Zagreb as well as in all other major cities throughout Croatian?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it may be very difficult for me to answer these military questions, but as far as I know the JNA was in many different areas and quite many were in Croatia at the time. As far as I know, there was a request for the JNA to withdraw. There was a lot of discussion and many decisions were taken to the effect that the JNA should withdraw. They were also in those occupied areas. There were people from the JNA there who were on Belgrade's payroll. I can't say exactly where the JNA was, but it was at any rate also in Croatia carrying out military operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the JNA plumb in the middle of Zagreb at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think they were still in their Zagreb barracks and probably they were still occupying facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Croatian army, did it exist at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have seen, police forces had been established which had military powers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The criterion of territory control, was it satisfied by the fact that Croatia had over two-thirds of its territory under control at the time, having obtained all the attributes of an independent state?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the best part of Croatia territory, but it's not about the quantity. The essential thing is that the international community recognised this as an act of cooperation. And many calls were issued for the JNA paramilitary units and the paramilitary units to withdraw from those occupied areas and that these occupied areas should be returned to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you've been able to establish in the meantime. You say the international community established an act of occupation?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, when, why, what, how?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to the general assembly resolution 49/43, which the title of the resolution is: "The situation in the occupied territories." And it refers to the Republic of Croatia -- it refers to the areas where there were those paramilitary units backed by the JNA. And where later the peacekeeping forces were installed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this resolution adopted, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it applies to which period of time exactly?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't state specifically which period of time. This went on for years since 1991. An attempt was made to prevent the spread of this situation, and that's why peacekeeping forces were sent to the area. There was an agreement that was concluded between Croatia and the UN. There was no third party to this agreement about the deployment of peacekeeping forces. Croatia had been internationally recognised and was in charge of those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which agreement was that and when was it signed?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the agreement on the -- the so-called SOFA, status of force agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was signed quite late on, actually, because negotiations had been underway for a long time as to the precise terms of the agreement, but Croatia was the only party in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year was the agreement signed in?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the peacekeeping forces, pursuant to an agreement reached with Croatia, had arrived a lot earlier, the agreement was only signed and concluded just before they left, which I believe was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the peacekeeping forces arrive in Yugoslavia towards the end of 1991, pursuant to which specific decision?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a series of agreements. There was a series of agreements. It wasn't only one decision that the whole thing hinged upon. It was a Croatian decision, no doubt, but also representatives of the UN wanted all the other parties to agree on that, all the other parties that could contribute to the conflict spreading throughout the area. Peacekeeping forces are usually sent to peaceful areas where there is no conflict, so the first thing was to preserve peace. And that's why other parties had to be included in these negotiations and not only the Republic of Croatia, but it is quite certain that the whole thing was about Croatian territory, about the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And later documents clearly confirmed this, especially documents such as resolution 815 of the UN security council as well as this resolution concerning occupied areas. These clearly indicate that these are Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which resolution of the Security Council was it and when was this resolution adopted, pursuant to which the peacekeeping forces arrived in Yugoslavia? Is there a reference to another perhaps in that resolution in addition to Yugoslavia. What exactly does the resolution say and when did it come into force, this resolution pursuant to which the peacekeeping forces were sent to Yugoslavia and arrived in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your previous question --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my present question.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was pursuant to an invitation of President Mesic. I know that he wrote to them, but there were several factors that decided the matter. I can't specify which resolution it was. I don't remember the number of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year was it adopted in?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was early 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there talk of Yugoslavia in that resolution? Is there talk of the arrival of the peacekeeping forces in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia at the time -- well, Serbia and Montenegro were still called Yugoslavia at the time, therefore the name Yugoslavia was still circulated. But this does not mean that Yugoslavia was the same thing as Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pursuant to that resolution, the peacekeeping forces, did they arrive in Serbia and Montenegro or in the part of Yugoslavia called Croatia or referred to as Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly arrived in Croatian territory, in the state of Croatia. And there was an agreement that was signed later, which refers to the Republic of Croatia. The state of Croatia signed that agreement and no other state but Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the 1994 agreement we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please allow me. I'm talking about the Security Council resolution, pursuant to which UNPROFOR was sent to Yugoslavia and deployed throughout the UNPA zones the Croatia. Were these forces sent to Yugoslavia also or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure because I don't remember the exact wording of the resolution, but what I believe is supremely relevant is that the forces were deployed in Croatian territory in the state of Croatia. Because this agreement -- there were no other parties to it but Croatia. Croatia was the only party to this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which leads you to conclude -- that one of your conclusions is that even following the arrival of these forces in 1991, Croatia was an independent and sovereign state -- the agreement was signed three years later --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my submission that -- and we know when Croatia became an independent state quite definitively and officially on the 8th of October. And I stick to that in all of my submissions. I stick to that fact. The peacekeeping forces arrived in Croatia. Whatever was being discussed in terms of Yugoslavia was with the sole aim of getting the other players involved in order to help preserve peace and keep the conflict from spreading. But we know that Yugoslavia was greatly involved in those other areas at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Security Council was less than accurate or perhaps unfamiliar with the situation on the ground when sending forces to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I mean to say. I don't have the wording in front of me so I can't tell you what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you what it says is that these forces are being deployed in Yugoslavia or being sent to Yugoslavia, does that mean that the security council was less than accurate as well as the Croatian parliament a while ago?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly I can't say, because I don't have the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in what capacity did Stipe Mesic invite UNPROFOR to come to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that he wrote a letter, but that was not the only document that was sent to the UN at the time in terms of requesting assistance for the situation to be resolved. He may have, but I can't say now because I don't have -- I don't have the document here and I did find this in one of the documents. He was one of the first to address, perhaps even in his official capacity as president of the presidency, most probably I assume, because he himself was not permitted to go about his duties. Nor did he have the power to issue any regulations or orders which the JNA would have followed and obeyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Stipe Mesic, as president of the presidency of the SFRY, calls on the peacekeeping forces of the UN to come to Yugoslavia, pursuant to which a resolution was adopted by the Security Council on sending the peacekeeping forces to the Republic of Croatia. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. He was one of those who sent out warnings and he said that this would be a good idea. But we know that before the peacekeeping forces were sent, there had been a lot of negotiations between mediators and people from the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to answer this in one sentence if possible. In what official capacity did Stipe Mesic call on the UN forces to come to Yugoslavia? Was he speaking as president of the presidency of the SFRY? Please, it's a yes or no question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is: I don't have the document in front of me so I don't know what the date is that the document bears. Those were still early days and I assume that he was president of the presidency, but I can't be sure. I can't say with certainty, and dates are of great importance to this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if it was after the 8th of October, 1991, that he called on the UN forces to come to Yugoslavia, what would you say then?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing really. We know that he lingered around for a while. But then following the decision of the 8th of October, some -- the actions taken by the officials on the behalf of the Republic of Croatia were declared null and void.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for example, in December, this call by Stipe Mesic to the UN forces in November was declared null and void. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant to say. I am still saying that the UN forces did not come simply because Mesic had invited them. He warned about the possibility of the UN forces being deployed in the area, but it was not merely on the basis of his call. This was pursuant to an agreement between the Croatian president and the officials in the Republic of Croatia, and later on in the game, even Belgrade agreed to play along with this. Pursuant to the Vance Owen Plan there was consensus for this to improve the situation. But the original agreement had been with the state of Croatia, with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the signatories of the Vance Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, because it's been a long time since I last looked at that particular document, the Vance Owen Plan. Whether it has anything to do with -- whether there are any specific signatories, I'm afraid I can't say who they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the date of this plan?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was just before the peacekeeping forces arrived in late 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did Cyrus Vance negotiate with the authorities in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to prevent the clashes from spreading. The peacekeeping forces were deployed pursuant to Article 6, not Article 7, so there had to be peace for the peacekeeping forces to be deployed because they were, after all, peacekeeping, not peace making forces. But the situation was delicate and there were innumerable violations of ceasefire. Agreements had been signed. But the conflict kept on escalating. The tensions kept on mounting and a way needed to be found to pacify the JNA and the authorities in Belgrade who -- which were in control of the JNA for the situation to be kept relatively stable for the mandate of the UN peacekeeping forces to be as brief and as successful as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you perhaps remember that the chief negotiator on the part of the federal states in these negotiations was the prime minister who originally hailed from Croatia, Ante Markovic, and the foreign officer -- the head of foreign office, Budimir Loncar, that is as the UN forces were being deployed?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know it was the Croatian authorities who did most of the negotiations, because the arrival was in Croatian territory. But there was an attempt at the time to get the federal authorities to play along, especially the JNA -- the JNA being the chief reason that war operations had broken out in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at tab 9, opinion number 3. If you look at number 3 -- item 3 of opinion number 3 -- item 2, rather, says first, second, and third. So the section marked as third and then the last paragraph of that section. Saying: "This principle," and it's a reference to the principle of resolving border-related issues, "should be that much easier to apply between the republics, pursuant to Article 2, 4, and 5 of the constitution of the SFRY, establishing the inviolability of republican territories and that the borders cannot be changed without consent from the republics." Is this the same document that we discussed as -- in reference to January and the same document that the initiative of the Montenegrin assembly is based upon?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This opinion speaks of republican borders having become international borders, and this is something that Croatia always advocated and was in favour of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now please look at tab 10. Madam, can you please tell me why the United States of America only recognised Croatia in April of 1992 and not earlier?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've spoken about recognition and as Badinter said it's a questio facti. Now, why did the United States only recognise Croatia at such a late stage in the process? Well, it's not for me to say. I don't know. I assume there were reasons, but I do not believe that this piece of information is in any way relevant to the status of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Latvia had recognised Croatia on the 30th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why were then diplomatic relations only established as late as March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, establishing diplomatic relations, this was not exactly the first thing that was done. This very much depended on the situation. There were precious few people working on that at the ministry, very few professionals who worked on these tasks that were essential for organising this new state. They were trying to tackle the most important issues first, the most urgent issues. So this late date at which diplomatic relations were established was -- with Latvia. It doesn't anything in itself. We did not have that many relations with Latvia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Croatia perhaps waiting for its diplomatic professionals to return from Belgrade so that they could then proceed and reinforce their own diplomacy?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was the case because there were very few professional diplomats in Belgrade. Perhaps there were about 20 of us Croatians working in Belgrade at the time. There were also administrative staff and personnel and people and professionals who were not dealing with this kind of issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at this table here. You have it in front of you now so it should be much easier for you to look at and it shouldn't take much time. How many countries had recognised Croatia by the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is not very useful, not very helpful. So now when it look at it, it's very difficult to say. It's in the alphabetic order. Once upon a time, it was chronology that was used to draw these up. Which date did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too many countries at any rate. Perhaps five or six, just by looking at it in very perfunctory way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please have a closer look. It shouldn't take more than several minutes.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may prove a bit more difficult. We talked about Slovenia, Latvia. Back in December I know there was Ukraine, Iceland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, please can you look at the table and refresh your memory, this column that says: "Recognition." Can you tell me, who had Croatia been recognised by by the 6th of December, 1991, which specific countries?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th of December, I'm not sure why the reference is to that specific date, why is this date particularly relevant, I'm not certain about that. My question is why the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, can you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found Lithuania and Slovenia by the date you gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. As you refer to five or six different states, is this table perhaps inaccurate, the statistics given here?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My answer was in reference to December. Perhaps I misunderstood your question, because I know that throughout 1991 about five or six states recognised Croatia. That was how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could please look at tab 11. Can you please look at the first document. This document by the Holy See, yes -- no, the first document is -- just a minute, please. So this letter by the Holy See dated the 13th of January, 1991, and another document dated the 20th of December, 1991. Can you please look at the one dated the 20th of December, paragraph 1 of that letter. It reads: "The Holy See is inclined to recognise Croatia as an independent and sovereign state pursuant to international norms on the condition that the conditions listed below are met." Tell me please, Madam, why is it that the Holy See at this point in time conditions its recognition upon the meeting of the requirements? Does that mean that the requirements had not been met by that time?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Holy See was merely setting out the same conditions as the European Community had before in their rules, the so-called Hague rules, those that had been set out in The Hague rules. Therefore, this is merely a repetition of the same thing that Europe had requested of all the new states coming into being in the area. This does not mean that the requirements had not been met, because had they not been met they could not have possibly been complied with in the few days before the final international recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me then why the Holy See did not simply recognise the Republic of Croatia as an independent state, but rather in reply to a letter by the Republic of Croatia later the answer, the reply of the Holy See is that there will be recognition once conditions have been met?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way they go about these things. They have their own diplomacy and they reiterated the same thing in this letter, that conditions needed to be complied with in order for a state to be internationally recognised. A very short time after Croatia was indeed recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But certainly they knew full well whether Croatia had met the requirements or not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by the time they granted Croatia full recognition, obviously their belief was that the requirements had been met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the letter dated the 20th of December, Madam?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what they were or were not familiar with at the time. It's only a matter of my interpretation and your interpretation now, is it? The fact is that Croatia was recognised by the Holy See on the 30th of January, which means that the general belief was Croatia had met all the requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at the supreme council of the Republic of Lithuania of the 30th of July, 1991. Do you treat this letter as a letter recognising the Republic of Croatia, because you mentioned a whole ago that Lithuania recognised Croatia on the 30th of July, 1991. Is this the letter 30th?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Yes, it has been registered as such. This is the fact which has been registered here. Lithuania recognised it on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at these decisions here. The supreme council of Lithuania passed a decision to recognise the legitimacy of the aspirations of the Republic of Croatia and a self-determination as an expression of its sovereign power. First of all, to establish contact with a view to reviewing the possibilities for establishing permanent diplomatic relations. So do you treat this aspirations as an intergovernmental act of recognition? Is this the way recognition is carried out of a state in diplomatic practice and language, in these words, in these formulations?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already mentioned last time, counsel. You should recall that a higher stage in the conclusion of agreements on diplomatic recognition is actually implied, because if the government of Lithuania was tasked with establishing contacts with the Republic of Croatia, an order to establish diplomatic relations, permanent, and other relations with the Republic of Croatia, that absolutely means that this contains implicit recognition, because this is a much higher stage of relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this means again that the text of the supreme council of Lithuania is not precise enough?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true. It is very precise. It in fact reinforces this recognition of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do these words aspirations of the Republic of Croatia mean?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it doesn't -- that there isn't -- first of all, it means that there is no doubt at all that this is recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item 1 means what?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it recognises -- or either the fact that Croatia has achieved its sovereignty is an expression of its legitimate aspirations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the word aspiration mean?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that it requires no interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, how was the parliament of the Republic of Croatia constituted in December 1991? What bodies comprised the parliament of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obviously constituted on the basis of the constitution which was then in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I haven't been clear enough, I shall repeat my question. What was the composition of the parliament of the Republic of Croatia? What bodies did it comprise?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It contained two chambers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What two chambers were these?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the house of representatives and the house of counties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind, Madam, as to go back to tab 8 and take a look at, for instance, document 1685. So this is a document, the content of which does not -- is not of the essence right now. But it says: "Decree on promulgating and on the use of flats, I hereby promulgate the law on the temporary use of flats which the parliament of the Republic of Croatia adopted decisions on the chamber of associated labour on the 4th of December, 1991. The chamber of municipalities on the 4th of December, 1991. And the sociopolitical chamber on the 4th of December, 1991. The 9th of December, President Franjo Tudjman."

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, definitely in 1991 there existed a constitution of the Republic of Croatia, and this law was adopted in December 1991. But the law had not been passed on the 4th of December, 1991. So that they worked according to the regulations which were in existence -- no, I'm sorry. It hadn't been passed by the year 1990, and we are now talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a law from December 1991 or is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it obviously states here that it is a law from 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it -- what is written on it? What are the bodies -- or rather, in it, what are the bodies, what are the chambers, of the parliament of Croatia in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the chamber -- that the constitution of the Republic of Croatia envisaged these two chambers bicameral parliament. Now, whether in the very beginning only these two chambers had been foreseen is something I cannot recall because I don't have the constitutional text before me. I cannot say with precision. I know that in the first text of the constitution there were some provisions, but whether these provisions existed in the first text -- but I do know that very soon the constitutional text envisaged these two chambers, the house of representatives and the house of counties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, is it written here that in December 1991, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia had these three chambers which are indicated here. Just please say yes or no. Let us not waste our time.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, I'm not versed in detailing constitutional matters. It is so stated here, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia from 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the Official Gazette, but I really have to see what this is about. Because I'm unprepared to reply in connection with this document. I cannot give you a proper interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that there is a mistake there in terms of the bodies of the chambers comprised within the parliament of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that there is a mistake, but I would have to consult the constitutional text and the relevant documents which were obtained at the time to be able to give you a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will help you now. Please revert to tab 4 and take a look at decision 872. And please take a look at the signature affixed to that decision, and that is the constitutional decision that we have already reviewed. Is there a mistake there perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Obviously in the first stage of the constitution, these chambers existed; evidently this is so. But what I was saying was that I'm quite certain that there was a provision that existed in the constitution of Croatia for some time until it was abolished and the counties' chamber was introduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try once again. In December 1991, did the chamber of the republic of -- the parliament of the Republic of Croatia consist of a chamber of sociopolitical communities, of municipalities, and of associated labour?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is written so here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had told me so ten minutes ago, we would have saved a lot of breath and a lot of time. Please tell me: This composition of the parliaments of the Republic of Croatia, had it existed as such since the constitution of 1974 and was not changed until the 1991 constitution?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: These chambers had existed before as well, but the manner of elected representatives to these chambers and whether that had changed is something I cannot say. And whether the criteria had changed for election, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the composition of the chamber of the -- sorry, parliament of the Republic of Croatia the same in 1974 and in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What matters is the procedure of elections and the criteria. This has to be taken into consideration. I cannot tell you that it was composed in the same way, but the names of the chambers are certainly the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why are these chambers the same? Why had nothing changed when a new constitution was taken, if this was a new state, if the circumstances were new and had changed, why did they retain the chamber of associated labour within the parliament of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This still doesn't mean anything. The designation of the chamber means nothing. The -- it is a fact that the new constitution had new provisions, and it is also a fact that in a legal system which is evolving, institutes do not crop up overnight. They are also evolving. So if the names of the chambers remain the same, that is not really of some specific gravity in terms of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, the composition of the chambers in a state parliament, can it only change if a constitutional change is introduced? This is not a matter of evolution. These are the very foundations of the state we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. These chambers were composed pursuant to the new constitution in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any continuity in terms of how the Croatian parliament was organised in relation to 1974? Is there a complete continuity in terms of how the highest supreme state organ was composed, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because there is no continuity in the way the authorities were organised. We can't only talk about the parliament and the names of the chambers. We know if nothing else the constitution of 1990 introduced the -- presidential system, therefore there was no complete continuity in the way the authorities were organised in Croatia, at least not in the same way that you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to ask you again: Was the Croatian parliament organised the same way back in 1974 and in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the names of the chambers, yes, but I can't say with any degree of certainty that the whole parliament was organised the same way. I should go back to documents to ascertain something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the names and the composition of the chambers?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered this in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Honourable Trial Chamber what the chamber of associated labour means.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That chamber is composed of representatives of employees who work for employers of any kind or under employers of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that associated labour and the relevant terminology is a classic example of how things were organised in communist Yugoslavia after 1974, the very foundations on which the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia arrested the concept of associated labour that unfortunately was tried only in that country and no where else. But it was still in place in Croatia in 1991, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is the very concept of associated labour that represented a mechanism or a bridge, if you like, a bridge between the communist system and the socialist system later on, for a transition to a more contemporary system. This was the idea, at least. There were to be collective contracts and the representative of the two parties to these contracts, employees and employers, were to agree on terms. That was the idea. It was a different idea back then and it was a relatively modern idea. It is not a communist idea as such. It is quite subversive in terms of communism, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have any such thing as associated labour in Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the same form. You can't find it in the same form anywhere in the area. But it was an interesting idea back then, and the West seemed interested in the idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your submission that communist Yugoslavia did not rest on the foundations of associated labour?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was never actually called communist Yugoslavia, but rather socialist Yugoslavia, at least to the best of my knowledge. And one of the foundations at a later stage, but the stage we are talking about is the stage where local communities -- the importance of local communities is being underlined and the local communities are being given more and more rights. It was in this context that the concept of associated labour gained currency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope everyone can understand what you're talking about. Tell me briefly, please, at tab 12. If you look at the last portion of that tab. Tell me, Madam, in your statement and in your testimony before this Court, you talked about there being a discontinuity, as you say, or rather - I shall quote you - "that there are new state structures in the Republic of Croatia and new legislation." A while ago we saw that in terms of the organisation of the supreme bodies of a state in Croatia there was continuity after all. So this discontinuity you're talking about, how did that come about in the area of -- for example, the law on criminal procedure. Does Croatia have a new law on criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia had kept its republican law until then, and then adopted its own law. Obviously amendments are being made to these laws, which is the case in all states where the legal systems are still evolving. Definitely you can't say there was discontinuity just because you've looked at the names of these three bodies and the names have changed. If nothing, the authorities themselves are set up in a different way in relation to what the executive council used to be in the former period. The role of the president is different and there is a whole series of new bodies, new authorities, that changed. So perhaps there is not a complete -- this is not a case of complete discontinuity, but obviously now we are facing a different system and different state structures that are now in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, on the 8th of October, 1991, which amendments were made to the federal law on criminal procedure? It's important to underline this, because there was the republican law on criminal procedure and the federal law on criminal procedure. What changes were made, except for the fact where it used to read "SFRY," now it read the "Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write this law and I am not an expert on this law, so I can't talk about any essential changes to this law. But I don't think it really matters. I think minor changes were made and later amendments were added. Sometimes you had to adapt the legal system, were it only in terms of names. It doesn't mean that all the provisions concerning criminal procedure were necessarily bad in relation to the new situations that had arisen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was changed in terms of the law on executive procedure, in addition to the name of the law itself?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same question as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the law on litigation? These are key laws, used to be key laws, in the SFRY, these three laws?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not an expert on these branches of the law. I'm sure there were a number of changes. I can't say for sure because I'm no expert on this. Obviously changes were made and some fundamental institutions after all had changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to look at the title page of the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia dated the 8th of October, 1991. The ERN 09426265. I'm not sure if an English translation of that document is available, but if you could please have a look. Have you located the document?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at document 1294, 1295, and further. All these documents seem to indicate -- it says: "Law on the adoption of the criminal law, law on the adoption of the law on criminal procedure, law on adoption of the law on litigation." What sort of discontinuity do you see there in terms of the laws? We see clearly that all of the laws were adopted without any changes being made.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is simply not true. These are not only laws on adoption. I said previously in my testimony that new laws were being adopted, firstly. Secondly, some of the existing laws were being adopted, in part or in whole, depending on the specific provisions, and then there was the law on entry into force. We have -- all three of these examples are here in this issue of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, 1297, the law on litigious procedure, for example, the law on the adoption of the law on litigious procedure. What does it mean that the existing law of the SFRY was renamed as a law of the Republic of Croatia, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1297, if we had the text --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, if I just look at the title, it's very difficult for me to say what it's about. There are quite a number of provisions here. If I look further, I see that things are being adopted but not in full. The entire law, some things are discarded and some things are adopted, some things are reformulated. So this is not adoption in full, by no means. So many provisions are being changed. If you look closely at the wording of the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is being changed? What is being discarded, apart from the formal provisions of the law?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a number of things. There are several items about the adoption. There are 61 paragraphs of the law, and each one addresses changes, provisions being discarded, new wording being introduced. So there was no adoption in full, only in part. But this is perfectly normal. Every time you have a provision or a law that practically governs life in a state, you can't have the whole thing. You change some things. Technically speaking, it would have been impossible to adopt the whole thing in full. You have to adopt these things into the new system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fortunately we have these things in front of us so it should be relatively easy to ascertain what happened exactly. I have several questions left, and then I'll be over and done with this line of questioning. Can you look at binder 2, tab 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, a time. Firstly, how much longer do you see yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I would like to finish before the break -- before the next break that is, if I have your permission. I need five more minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the defence law dated the 20th of September, 1991. This is at tab 13. Can you please look at Article 190. That's binder 2. Tab 13. Is this not how it reads: "Conscripts, citizens of the Republic of Croatia, shall, as of the date of the entry into force of this law, not be sent for military service with the JNA outside Croatian territory." Does this not mean that pursuant to the law dated the 20th of September, 1991, Croatia still sends recruits to the JNA, to units deployed in Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the text in English. Can you please refer to the article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 190, paragraph 1, the law is dated the 20th of September, 1991, transitional provisions and concluding provisions. That's paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have that portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that as late as September 1991 Croatian conscripts are still being sent to JNA units throughout Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still can't seem to be able to locate that particular portion of the text, the law on defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is at tab 13 and there are two laws there. One is dated January and the other is dated September. The other law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't mean to intrude, Mr. Petrovic. One of the members of the Chamber has found page 01906185. It's actually stamped two-thirds if the way down the page. It's the gazette of the 20th of September, 1991, Article 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's right, that's right. Yes, the English translation. 190. That's at the top of the page in the English translation, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is Article 190, paragraph 1. My interpretation is that the JNA stationed outside the Republic of Croatia and that no conscripts will be sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat this last thing you said, the JNA being stationed outside Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my interpretation. It says that: "No conscripts will be sent to do their military service with the JNA outside the territory of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you a hand there. I'll read out the Croatian text to you so that may make it easier for you to understand. "Conscripts who are Croatian citizens as of the date of entry into force of this law shall not be sent to do their military service with the JNA outside the territory of the Republic of Croatia." Does that make it any easier for you now?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what do you expect me to do?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I expect you to confirm that pursuant to the law on defence dated 20th of September, 1991, conscripts from the Republic of Croatia were still being sent to JNA units that were stationed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think the law was adopted earlier. It was only made public as late as September when the JNA was still around. And it was precisely pursuant to this law that a new Croatian defence law was adopted. Therefore, I see nothing unusual about the fact that this remains the same and that no conscripts were being sent. There were war operations in the territory of the Republic of Croatia underway at the time. And it was out of the question to send any conscripts for service with the JNA outside the Croatian territory. I believe the law was actually adopted in the month of June originally, but it was published in the Official Gazette as late as September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I assist you with this, please? Look at Article 202, Madam.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This law shall enter into force on the day it is published in the Official Gazette, meaning the 20th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct. But originally the law was passed on the 26th of June, at which time every single day mattered, let alone months. The situation kept changing from day-to-day throughout that period of time; therefore, I am not surprised that this sort of wording should be included, "JNA stationed outside Croatian territory". Because the fact was the JNA was still in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, in September 1991, pursuant to the provisions of the law and pursuant to a law which was after all published in the Official Gazette on the 20th of September, 1991, does it not follow that conscripts from the Republic of Croatia were sent to do military service with JNA units stationed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that was the case. That was by no means the case. This was indeed stated in this particular provision of the law, but in practice conscripts were not any longer being sent to JNA units outside the Republic of Croatia. I know this from accounts of my friends whose sons were conscripts at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore you would say that this provision, like all -- many of the other provisions that we looked at today, and in your previous testimony, is a case of inaccurate wording?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think you're just misrepresenting the meaning of some of my answers. I'm not categorically stating that the wording of these provisions is inaccurate. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We will then have a break now and re-examination can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have some questions prepared for re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. Re-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Ambassador, in cross-examination you were asked some questions about the republican borders of the SFRY. In particular you were asked about the requirement under article 5 of the constitution of mutual agreement before the boundaries can be altered. The question is: Did the Croatian Republic ever seek to alter its land borders?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Republic of Croatia never sought to change its borders. Needless to say, it was prepared to accept negotiations to clarify any uncertainties in that regard. And in fact, it always sought for these borders of the former republic to be confirmed as international borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that in fact occur after the international recognition of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The borders were endorsed in keeping with the opinion of the Badinter Commission. However, there were negotiations about some technical details at some border points and stretches. Because simply speaking, for instance, between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no border disputes but there were some technicalities to be worked out in order to draw the border line in some areas where this was instances. And that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the borders remain more or less the same as they were when Croatia was part of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second area is: In cross-examination you told my learned colleague, Mr. Petrovic, that in particular in the Brussels declaration there was criticism of the violent intervention of the Serbian republic in Croatian affairs. I wish to direct you to a particular portion of Exhibit P20, which is tab 5. Can you please turn to tab 5 of the exhibit bundle in front of you. Is that the declaration to which you're referring, and that is the EU declaration of Yugoslavia of the 27th of August, 1991? About the fifth page in.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the declaration of the 27th of August. And it explicitly states that the fait accompli situation will not be accepted and that the Yugoslav army was in fact responsible for the situation which was obtaining [as interpreted] in the area. With particular emphasis on Serbia and everything that we already said before. It is mainly a condemnation of the forces of the JNA and of the Serbian forces and a condemnation of the paramilitary units for the situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Ambassador, another area. If you could just turn away from that one now. Defence counsel Mr. Petrovic also asked you whether republican laws were obliged to be in compliance with the SFRY constitution. Now, I want you to answer this as briefly as you possibly can, but in your view was there still a valid and federal constitutional -- sorry, federal constitutional structure in place in mid- to late-1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently, Yugoslavia was in a state of disintegration. That was -- has been noted so we cannot point the concrete date as which something stopped functioning. But generally the federal organs deteriorating in terms of the performance of their duties and functioning generally. This also was true of the laws. The laws were supposed to be in keeping with the constitutions of the republics and of course the federal constitution. However, no one could challenge the republican constitutions because they had precedence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic also asked you in cross-examination about the status of the FRY throughout 1991. My question is: Do you recall or know whether the FRY ever sought international recognition in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 19 -- not in 1991, but it was quite clear in Yugoslavia and to Yugoslavia that it was falling apart so that various statements inter alia in the memoirs of the then defence minister, Mr. Kadijevic [phoen], were given to this effect that a state was disintegrating and that the army would --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honours, we have to pause between. And I'm going to ask you to -- we're not recording at the moment, I have to ask you to go over that answer in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told that it may be three minutes or so for the system to be restored. Rather than go through all the formality of rising, I think we might just sit and wait in patience. Perhaps you might take the witness's attention back to where you were and continue with the evidence, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The answer will actually have been recorded. If Your Honours consider it necessary to have the question re --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. But I think you interrupted the Ambassador in mid-answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you were midway through your answer to a question about the FRY ever seeking international recognition in 1991. You said, I think, that they started to do it in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1991 -- you mean the SFRY, namely Serbia and Montenegro, it did not seek recognition in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it seek international recognition, and if so, was it as reported a successor state to the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very long time Serbia and Montenegro did not seek recognition, but considered themselves to be the only successor to the continuity of the former state. Of course all the other republics challenged this view. And not only that, but at the recommendation of the Security Council, the general assembly adopted a decision to the effect that Serbia and Montenegro had to apply for membership to the United Nations. It could not be the sole successor to the former Yugoslavia. And in the final analysis, they did apply for membership of the United Nations and are now a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question actually was: When did Serbia and Montenegro, as purporting to be the successor to the SFRY, seek international recognition? Admission to the United Nations is only one, as you appreciate, the things it could do. When did it start seeking international recognition?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can't say for -- for instance, in 1992 when they circulated a letter through the structures of the United Nations, at that point they became a different state, another state. It was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, rather than the previous SFRY. And at that time they requested to succeed to the SFRY as the only successor. But by that act, they did not seek recognition. They simply considered themselves to be the only successor state. To that effect, Serbia and Montenegro never sought international recognition by the date of succession after the dissolution of the former state, according to Badinter's opinion number one is the relevant date in that regard -- in the opinion number 11. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Madam Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit D11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- Madam Ambassador, can you just take a few seconds to familiarise yourself with this document you were shown in cross-examination and is an English language document dated the 18th of October, 1991. It contains certain conclusions about the federal presidency and you were questioned in relation to those. How many members did the federal presidency have by October 1991, just the number, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were eight members in the federal presidency, those representing all the republics and the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by October 1991, was the federal presidency still functioning effectively, that is to the extent it would be able to effectively regulate the affairs of the entire territory over which it claimed jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. This was a situation -- the situation of the impossibility of the presidents to function dated back to the -- to May 1991 when the -- these -- Croatian candidate who was to be appointed as president of the presidency was rejected. And that was because of Serbia's blockade -- rejection of this proposal. That is why the presidency was ineffectual. All the attempts to try and reinstitute some of the institutions were extremely important at that point because the Yugoslav People's Army had already started operating and was increasingly becoming an army of the Republic of Serbia, operating in the territories of other states. And all this in the absence of a functioning presidency and president of the presidency as the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the Prosecution's re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Alajbeg, may we thank you very much for your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May we thank you very much for your attendance here. But before you leave I would ask Judge Thelin to ask some questions on behalf of the Chamber. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Ambassador Alajbeg, just two minor questions. One goes to general character. We have been exposed, as you have, through many days now to the Official Gazette, which contains two dates. One is the date when a decision is taken by the institutions effective therein. And the second is the date when the gazette is published. I understand that the decision date is also a date when public coverage through print media or electronic media may happen so that the public would actually know some of the content before it is published in the gazette. That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Very often these documents which are secret were published immediately after adoption, but not in the Official Gazette. This is a known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: If we then move - and this is my second question - to the decisions taken on the 5th of December which we find in tab 8 - you don't have to go to the binder - the decisions I'm thinking of is the decision whereby the joint assembly dissociates itself, as it were, from functions in what is called the former federal republic. I'm thinking of the prime minister and of the Croat member of the presidency. Would you say that when that decision was taken, that media coverage of that was any other than decisions taken prior to that date? I'm thinking of the whole events from the referendum, to take a starting part, and then onwards in the autumn. Would that particular day and that decision need more coverage, or was it just covered as some of the other events were?

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in view of the fact that these were very senior officials in question, the decision did receive wide media coverage, as far as I can remember. But this came as no surprise to anyone because it was a well-known fact that these persons who worked in the federal bodies and hailed from the Republic of Croatia had had problems in their work for a long time before that. So that this only confirmed a situation that had already obtained and it was common knowledge in Croatia that one could not count on these bodies any longer nor any effective participation of Croatian interest in those bodies at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ambassador Alajbeg.

utterances.speaker: LJERKA ALAJBEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're most welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I trust that you will appreciate the importance of your evidence being concluded, and therefore the need for you to return, as you have today. May I indicate that your evidence is now formally concluded and you may leave and go about your other affairs. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Trial Chamber and the Presiding Judge very much. I believe that we did a useful job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Re, I look to you with the question in my mind whether it is convenient and practical to continue with the evidence of the part-heard witness at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To which I can only respond I'm entirely in the Trial Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness is here and available; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As I understand it, he should be. We of course haven't spoken to him. Mr. Usher should be able to tell us whether he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've temporarily lost Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are two witness rooms. One witness should be in one and one in the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic -- oh, it's Mr. Petrovic. I was going to ask whether it would be practical to conduct 25 minutes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this question should be answered by my learned friend and colleague. I wanted to use this time to ask a different question, to broach a different subject, just briefly, if I may be allowed. Or perhaps you would like Mr. Rodic to give the answer to the first question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I understood -- I did not understand the examination-in-chief of Witness Ciganovic to have been completed yesterday. My learned friend and colleague Mr. Re did not underline that. I think because the time ran out his examination-in-chief was interrupted. So perhaps he would first like to complete his examination-in-chief before I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long would you expect to be then?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I might finish; I might not. I mean, I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands. If we could use the available time, I'm sure it wouldn't hurt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the other matter you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is a matter on which I believe the Trial Chamber can exercise its authority and make our defendant's life more livable. What am I talking about? The rooms in which the accused, Mr. Strugar, has to stay while we are here in Courtroom II, the air-conditioning in the room is very weak and it's very difficult to switch off. So the fresh air hits Mr. Strugar directly in the neck and he has a lot of trouble with his neck. We would like the Trial Chamber, if possible, to ask the security section during breaks in Courtroom II to allow the accused to stay in the corridor just outside the room or the cell which is not far from here, not to be taken into the room, in other words, but rather to stay outside in the corridor during the break for these 20 minutes, for there to be put a chair that he can sit down on. I have managed to find out that this is indeed a real possibility, but only if the Trial Chamber orders this to be done. Exceptions can be made, I have been informed, in as far as an order has been issued by the Chamber for this to be done. Therefore, I would like to kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow for this to be done so that the pain of my client can be alleviated and so that he can sit outside in the corridor during the break. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing that matter to our attention, Mr. Petrovic. It would be unwise of the Chamber to make an order without first receiving some report or advice on the situation. But we will ask the court officer to make inquiries and let us have a view about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the -- we've lost him again. We need the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. I'm sorry you've had to wait so long, but we've now concluded the previous witness. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, it still applies. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ciganovic, yesterday when we were -- when you were giving your evidence about the death of Pavo Urban, you referred to your diagnosis -- of you being able to make a diagnosis on the basis of signs of haemorrhaging on his body. What are the signs of haemorrhaging that enabled you to make that diagnosis? And before you answer, can the witness please also be given access to MFI 70 and 71 from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When haemorrhaging is the cause of death or blood vessels are emptied out -- blood vessels in the body to the extent that this brings about a condition usually known as ischaemia of tissue and organs. And this is the cause of death -- the immediate cause of death. This happens while the body is still alive, because in order for haemorrhage to occur, the heart must still be functioning. When a dead body is injured, blood passively flows out of the injury but the blood vessels in the more remote sections of the body are not emptied out to the same extent as is the case when an injury is inflicted while the victim is still alive and therefore suffers haemorrhage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at photograph MFI 71, which is photo 74, which you told the Trial Chamber yesterday was a photo taken before you performed your autopsy. Are any signs of haemorrhaging visible in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this photograph you can't see any signs of haemorrhage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence yesterday was of your observation of blood flowing from the wound -- I'm sorry, damaged intestines and other abdominal organs and finding a fragment of an explosive device that caused the damage and haemorrhage as being the cause of death. Are you able, from that photograph, to see any of the blood within the abdomen?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, this is a poor photograph. From this particular angle, you can't see any blood in the abdomen and the photograph does not show blood that comes from the wound but dries up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to make your diagnosis and findings and find the fragment without -- sorry, with an external examination or did you also have to perform a partial internal examination?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out a partial internal examination in order to ascertain the extent of damage to internal organs and in order to locate the piece of explosive device lodged in the body. I also used other methods in order to ascertain the state that we usually refer to as death by haemorrhaging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber in lay terms what you mean by performing a partial examination -- internal examination.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you have a partial internal examination, if the wound itself is not wide enough so that you can insert your hand into the body cavity through the wound and look at the internal organs and the damage done, then you use a scalpel to widen the wound in order for you to be able to carry out this kind of examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to turn to the report which has been prepared, which you told the Trial Chamber yesterday is your report and an accurate record of the autopsy that you performed, and the examination of Mr. Urban which is person number 15. The relevant portion refers to rigor mortis extensive all over the body, skin pale, poorly visible livores mortis on the back. The following injuries were established on the front of the abdomen in the area of hip, which you changed to naval, explosive injury of the irregular shaped 5 centimetre diameter, compressed and torn intestine and abdomen organs, with lots of blood in the abdomen, what is the cause of death. Firstly, can you give the Trial Chamber a brief explanation of what is livores mortis and its significance here.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Livores mortis occur several hours after death on the lower parts of the body, the lower parts of the body facing the ground. Usually they occur on the back. The red blood -- the red blood corpuscles disintegrate and then haemoglobin penetrates skin. In haemorrhage these livores mortis are usually less apparent because there's less blood in the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you have to do to find the "compressed and torn intestine and abdomen organs with lots of blood in the abdomen"?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to open the wound and make it wider, and then through this opening I inspected the organs. I looked at the organs and I filled the organs with my fingers in order to ascertain what sort of damage had been inflicted. And I had to locate the device which caused such damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your opinion was that there was an explosive injury causing haemorrhaging leading to death. From your examination and your experience, which you outlined to the Trial Chamber yesterday, and your experience of examining many bodies with explosive injuries, was there anything else that you saw in this particular examination that you felt could have caused Mr. Urban's death?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another examination you performed on the day and is recorded in your report is that of the body of Tonco Skocko. That's number 11. Now, yesterday you were able to give details of the autopsy -- your autopsy of Mr. Urban without having to refer to your report, you said because you remembered who Mr. Urban was. Are you able to give those details to the Trial Chamber without -- in relation to Mr. Skocko without having to refer to your report, or do you need to go back to your report to refresh your memory as to the autopsy you performed? I'm only asking if you need to look at the report, that's all.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, I think I would probably need to look at the report to refresh my memory. I can't remember any details of this particular autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at the findings, and I also want to show you a photograph which is -- has a number on it which is 70 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, does that photograph with the large number 7-0 on the body correspond with --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph is the same as the description provided in the document that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the report to refresh your memory, can you please tell the Trial Chamber how you performed your autopsy on Mr. Skocko, what you did and what you found.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I performed the autopsy in a manner similar to that I applied in the previous case. I widened the opening of the wound, which you can see in this photograph, and I inspected the inside of the thorax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the wound you can see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on the front right side of the chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it correspond with the wound that you have recorded in your report, that is the wound in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find when you inspected the inside of Mr. Skocko's thorax?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ascertained that the right half of the -- the right lung had been damaged, torn by a fragment of an explosive device. The balance of the lung had been badly contused. The right side of the thorax was filled with blood. Further, I found signs of haemorrhaging on the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify it completely, are you saying that you performed a partial internal examination to make those findings?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your opinion as to the cause of Mr. Skocko's death, based upon your examination and experience?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based upon my examination and my experience, I concluded that the cause of death was haemorrhage. This was because I found empty blood vessels on the body's periphery and poorly visible livores mortis. The amount of blood in Mr. Skocko's body was not sufficient for him to go on living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report says at the end "there is a lot of blood in front of the chest. The cause of death: Explosive injury of the thorax with loss of blood." Why did you diagnose an explosive injury?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CIGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The injury itself on the surface and inside the body bore all the characteristics of an injury that had been caused by an explosive device. In the bottom of the injury itself I found a piece of an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Noting the time, might the photograph of Mr. Skocko also be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document MFI P72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient point, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, we must interrupt your evidence once more at this point to resume tomorrow.
